concepts.name: Definition and Chronological Placement of Megaliths in Indian Context
key_dimensions: Distinction between 'megalith' as a structural type vs. a cultural phase — trap: not all megaliths are prehistoric
Overlap with Iron Age periodization (~1500 BCE – 300 CE) and debate on whether Megaliths define a separate cultural stage
Comparison with European megalithic tradition (Neolithic) vs. Indian megalithic tradition (Iron Age) — a frequent UPSC trap
Protohistoric vs. Prehistoric classification of South Indian Megaliths

concepts.name: Geographical Distribution of Megalithic Cultures in India
key_dimensions: Core zone: South India — Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana
Extension into Deccan, Vidarbha, and Odisha — identifying region-specific megalith types
Northeastern India (Naga Hills, Khasi Hills) — living megalithic tradition vs. prehistoric megaliths (a critical distinction)
Absence or rarity in the Indo-Gangetic Plain — reason and significance for UPSC comparative questions

concepts.name: Typology of Megalithic Structures: Burial vs. Non-Burial
key_dimensions: Burial types: Dolmens, Cairn circles, Cists, Sarcophagi, Urn burials, Rock-cut caves — distinguishing features
Non-burial/commemorative types: Menhirs, Stone alignments, Stone circles (not all megaliths are tombs — UPSC trap)
Port-hole cist: unique feature indicating secondary burial practice
Hood-stone (capstone) structures vs. pit burials — structural differentiation

concepts.name: Dolmens: Structure, Distribution, and Funerary Significance
key_dimensions: Structure: Three or more upright stones supporting a horizontal capstone — distinction from trilithon
Dolmenoid cist vs. true dolmen — a frequently confused pair in UPSC options
Concentration in Kerala (Kerala dolmens locally called 'Muniyara') and Karnataka
Association with secondary burial practices and ancestor veneration

concepts.name: Cairn Circles and Rock-Cut Caves as Megalithic Burial Forms
key_dimensions: Cairn circle: Stone heap over burial pit, often with a peripheral ring — distinction from stone circle
Rock-cut caves (Pandav Leni type) in Maharashtra and Deccan — confusion with Buddhist rock-cut architecture (UPSC trap)
Cairns in Vidarbha region — Vidarbha Megalithic culture as a distinct sub-tradition
Relationship between cairn circles and iron-using communities

concepts.name: Menhirs: Symbolism, Distribution, and Living Tradition
key_dimensions: Definition: Single upright standing stone — not a burial structure (key distinction from dolmen)
Commemorative and territorial marker functions vs. purely funerary interpretation
Living menhir tradition among Naga tribes — bridge between prehistoric and ethnographic record
Menhirs vs. Victory pillars (Veerakkal/Hero stones) — overlap and distinction

concepts.name: Urn Burials and Their Significance in South Indian Megaliths
key_dimensions: Practice of placing skeletal remains in large ceramic urns — distinction from primary inhumation
Concentration in Tamil Nadu (Adichanallur is key site) — association with Sangam-age proto-Tamil culture
Types: single urn, paired urn (hat-shaped lid urn), terracotta sarcophagi
Grave goods in urn burials: iron tools, Black and Red Ware — cultural inference for UPSC

concepts.name: Adichanallur: A Key Megalithic Site and Its UPSC Significance
key_dimensions: Location: Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu — on the banks of Tamiraparani river
Urn burial site with over 169 urns excavated — one of the largest megalithic cemeteries
Evidence of early Tamil script/symbols on pottery — potential link to proto-Tamil identity (controversial)
Recent re-excavation (ASI, 2019) and its significance — contemporary relevance angle

concepts.name: Black and Red Ware (BRW) as Diagnostic Pottery of Megalithic Culture
key_dimensions: Technique: wheel-made, fired in specific oxidizing/reducing conditions — black on inside and rim, red on outside
Distribution: South India Megaliths, also found in later Painted Grey Ware (PGW) sites — UPSC overlap trap
BRW vs. Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) — chronological and geographic distinction
BRW as a cultural marker linking Iron Age communities across Deccan and South India

concepts.name: Iron Technology and Its Association with Megalithic Cultures
key_dimensions: Megaliths in India are predominantly Iron Age phenomena — iron tools (swords, axes, arrowheads) as grave goods
Debate: Did iron technology spread with megaliths or vice versa? — chicken-and-egg problem in historiography
Iron smelting evidence at megalithic sites: Hallur, Brahmagiri, Piklihal
Contrast with Chalcolithic cultures of Deccan — megalithic Iron Age representing a technological leap

concepts.name: Brahmagiri Excavation and Mortimer Wheeler's Contribution
key_dimensions: Excavated by Mortimer Wheeler (1947) — one of the first systematic megalithic excavations in India
Three cultural phases identified: Neolithic, Megalithic (Iron Age), and Early Historic — stratigraphic significance
Evidence of transition from Neolithic-Chalcolithic to Megalithic culture at a single site
Location: Karnataka (Chitradurga district) — often confused with other Karnataka sites (UPSC trap)

concepts.name: Secondary Burial Practice and Port-Hole Cist Technology
key_dimensions: Secondary burial: body first exposed/decomposed, then bones collected and placed in megalith — distinction from primary burial
Port-hole (circular opening) in cist walls enabling repeated access for secondary burials
Social interpretation: ancestor worship, clan burial grounds, collective identity
Port-hole cists concentrated in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh — geographic specificity for MCQs

concepts.name: Megalithic Hero Stones (Veerakkal) and Their Historiographical Significance
key_dimensions: Hero stones: commemorative slabs erected for warriors — bridge between megalithic tradition and historical period
Earliest hero stones (3rd century BCE onwards) in South India — overlap with Sangam literature
Iconographic panels on hero stones: battle scenes, celestial motifs — art history angle
Distinction: Hero stones are NOT strictly megalithic burials — they are commemorative (UPSC trap on 'types of megaliths')

concepts.name: Northeastern Indian Megalithic Tradition: Living Megalithism
key_dimensions: Khasi, Garo, Naga tribes — continuing tradition of erecting megaliths for social/commemorative purposes
Function: feast-of-merit platforms, territorial markers, memorials — NOT primarily funerary
Ethnographic parallel used to interpret prehistoric megaliths — methodological significance
Key distinction: Northeast megaliths are 'living tradition' (ethnographic present), not prehistoric relics — frequent UPSC confusion point

concepts.name: Vidarbha Megalithic Culture as a Distinct Regional Sub-Tradition
key_dimensions: Geographic focus: Nagpur and Wardha districts of Maharashtra
Characteristic feature: Cairn circles with central pit burials — different from South Indian cist graves
Excavated sites: Naikund, Mahurjhari — specific site-type associations for MCQs
Cultural connection: Possibly linked to proto-Dravidian or early Deccan Iron Age communities — historiographical debate

concepts.name: Grave Goods and Social Stratification Inferences from Megalithic Burials
key_dimensions: Grave goods: iron weapons, bronze mirrors, gold ornaments, beads, pottery — differential distribution implies social hierarchy
Presence of horse equipment (bits, trappings) — evidence of horse-using warrior elite in Iron Age South India
Contrast: elaborate megaliths with rich goods vs. simple pit burials — two-tier social structure inference
Limitation: Over-interpretation of grave goods — methodological caution in historical reconstruction (Mains angle)

concepts.name: Origin Theories of Indian Megaliths: Diffusion vs. Independent Invention
key_dimensions: Diffusionist theory: Megaliths spread from Mediterranean/Middle East to India via sea or land routes
Independent invention theory: Similar funerary needs produce similar structures independently (Gordon Childe vs. local school)
Gordon Childe's diffusionist model vs. S.B. Deo and R.K. Momin's indigenous origin argument
Current scholarly consensus: Polycentric origin — no single source, each region evolved its own tradition

concepts.name: Relationship Between Megalithic Culture and Early Tamil/Dravidian Identity
key_dimensions: Megalithic phase in Tamil Nadu as the archaeological correlate of early Sangam-age society
Pottery inscriptions (graffiti marks) at megalithic sites as precursors to Tamil-Brahmi script — controversial claim
Adichanallur and Kodumanal as sites linking megalithic material culture with proto-Tamil communities
Debate: Are Dravidian-speaking peoples the builders of South Indian megaliths? — linguistic-archaeological correlation trap

concepts.name: Transition from Megalithic to Early Historic Period in South India
key_dimensions: Continuity evidence: BRW pottery, iron use, and burial customs persisting into early historic period
Emergence of megalithic-built settlements (not just cemeteries) — Kodumanal as a trading-cum-craft site
Arrival of Northern influences (NBPW, punch-marked coins, Mauryan contacts) marking the transition
The 'megalithic' label ends but the people continue — cultural continuity vs. periodization trap for UPSC

concepts.name: Key Excavated Megalithic Sites and Their Distinctive Features (Site-Type Matrix)
key_dimensions: Adichanallur (TN): Urn burials, BRW, early Tamil graffiti — most frequently cited in UPSC
Brahmagiri (Karnataka): Wheeler's excavation, three-phase stratigraphy, cist graves
Hallur (Karnataka): Early iron smelting evidence, overlap with Neolithic-Chalcolithic
Kodumanal (TN): Megalithic + early historic craft/trade site — semi-precious stone bead industry; Vikramkhol (Odisha) for northern extension
